China is not trying to catch up on AI chips anymore. It is building an entirely different AI computing stack.

Huawei unveiled the Atlas 960E SuperPod this week — a system with UnifiedBus architecture designed to scale from thousands of NPUs toward million-NPU clusters. This is not a chip refresh. It is a complete alternative to the NVIDIA-dominated infrastructure that powers virtually every Western frontier AI model.

The same week, Meta announced Petal, a transatlantic AI cable spanning 4,300 miles between the U.S. and France, carrying roughly double the capacity of today's leading cables.

The AI race has moved beneath the models. It is now about the physical and architectural foundations that determine who can build and deploy AI at scale.

For CTOs, this introduces real bifurcation risk into infrastructure planning. If the global AI compute stack splits into Western and Eastern ecosystems, vendor lock-in and supply chain resilience stop being procurement topics and become board-level concerns.

For CEOs with global operations, compute partnerships, data residency requirements, and even talent strategies may increasingly be shaped by which infrastructure stack a region adopts.

The companies treating AI infrastructure as interchangeable are underestimating the most consequential strategic variable in play right now.
